newsitem.title: POLAND: Illness saves Poland's Jaruzelski from trial.
newsitem.headline: Illness saves Poland's Jaruzelski from trial.

text.p: A Polish court has ruled that former communist ruler Wojciech Jaruzelski is too ill to stand trial for the shootings of protesters by security forces in 1970 when he was defence minister, a judge said on Tuesday.

"Doctors have found that in his current state of health Wojciech Jaruzelski cannot take part in a trial outside his place of residence," Wlodzimierz Brazewicz, a judge of the provincial court in the coastal city of Gdansk, told Reuters.

In 1970 troops and police shot dead at least 44 people protesting in Polish coastal cities against food price rises decreed by the undemocratic ruling communists. Almost 200 were seriously wounded and about 1,000 badly beaten.
General Jaruzelski, 74, who lives in Warsaw, is among 12 former ministers and senior officials who are due to face a long-delayed trial over the issue in Gdansk.
But the judge said only seven would now take part, including the then deputy prime minister Stanislaw Kociolek.
He said doctors had diagnosed that Jaruzelski had illnesses of the kidneys, eyes and spine and bouts of depression -- all of which would take six or eight months to treat.
"The changes caused by the illnesses are lasting and do not suggest a return by the accused to full psychological and physical fitness," said Brazewicz.

Jaruzelski, who denies responsibility for the 1970 shootings, unsuccessfully applied earlier this year to be tried before Poland's State Tribunal in Warsaw, which deals with alleged wrongdoings by high officials.
Delays in starting the trial, years after the 1989 fall of communism, have infuriated many veterans of the struggle for democracy and especially those in the Solidarity union.
They allege that such delays may be due to the dominance of ex-communists in the coalition government since 1993.

Last year a parliamentary committee dominated by the ex-communists decided that Jaruzelski should not stand trial for his 1981 martial law decree to crush Solidarity, the Soviet bloc's first free trade union. Jaruzelski argues that he took the decision from patriotic motives to avert the threat of Russian military intervention. Opinion surveys show that many Poles accept these arguments.
